The descriptor matrix is a 2-plane long matrix describing the start and end coordinates (in the incoming matrix) of matches and back references returned by jit.str.regexp. Each row of the descriptor matrix represents a match, and the data appears in pairs across the row: the first pair represents the start and end of the basic match [the data output from the substrings outlet]; each additional pair represents a back reference [the data output from the back references outlet].

setting a new text color depending on the status of the text (unmatched = black, principal match = red, backrefs are progressively lighter blue/green)

In general use, the jit.str.regexp object does not give any information about the context of matches -- where they appear within the input matrix. Since the descriptor matrix reports that information, we can use it to colorize different parts of the matrix according to whether they were matched, and how (principal match, backref), providing a clear visual display of how the input matrix was analyzed.

\\.(?:jpg|gif) searchs for a period (.) followed by jpg or gif. We need to use parenthesis to isolate the jpg and gif terms from the rest of the expression, but we don't want a back reference generated. (?: declares that these parens are being used only for isolation, and does not create a backref
This sequence will continue (*) until it hits the next search term (? makes the * ungreedy -- it stops at the first instance of the next term)
[\\w|/|:|.]*? searches for a sequence composed of 'word' characters or the symbols /, : or .

This patch will download the Cycling '74 home page to a Jitter matrix using jit.uldl (you can view the HTML in the jit.textfile object). It then uses jit.str.regexp to parse the HTML to extract any jpeg or gif files found on the page. These file names are then converted into Max messages and sent in sequence to jit.uldl, downloading each one.
anchored: the RE is constrained to match only at the start of the incoming matrix.
extra: of virtually no use. Causes an error when an undefined escape character is in an RE.
Here, we specify that we'd like the analysis to be case insensitive.
ungreedy: inverts the 'greediness' of the search pattern, so that the ? metacharacter forces greed.

The first 4 options may also specified with a regular expression (advanced or not), by using the (?) symbol. For example /abc/i and (?i)abc are equivalent. If you only want a portion of your regular expression to be affected by an option, you must specify it as a backref (e.g. a((?i)bc) in which only bc is case insensitive).
These may be combined (e.g. /theRE/iS will be a studied, case insensitive analysis).
study: analyses the RE further for increased speed while matching.
dollar endonly: the dollar ($) metacharacter in an RE matches only at the end of the input matrix. Otherwise, it matches immediately before the finial character if it is a newline.
extended: permits comments in RE strings. See the included documents for more information.
dotall: the period (.) metacharacter in an RE matches all characters, including newlines. Otherwise, newlines will not match a period.
multiline: start and end of line specifiers match characters immediately before or after newlines

In a substitution string, use '%%n' to create a literal '%n', where n is a digit. Otherwise, that combination is read as a backreference.
You must use double \\ to create a single backslash . To create a literal \, use \\\\.
Things to keep in mind when you write regular expressions:
alternative (e.g. cats|dogs will find match 'cats' or 'dogs')
… will be remembered as a backreference— it may be referred to in a substitution string as %n, where n is the position of the left parenthesis in left-to-right order.
… appears once or not at all
